statement: A square with sides of 6 cm is cut into two equal rectangles. What is the perimeter of one of the rectangles?

choices.misconception: I halved the perimeter of the square, 24 cm, but the cut adds a new 6 cm side to each rectangle.
I gave the perimeter of the whole square instead of one rectangle.
I added the cut to the perimeter of the square, $24 + 6 = 30$, which is the length of all the lines, not one rectangle.
I added the perimeters of both rectangles together instead of giving one.

hints: Draw it. How long and how wide is one rectangle?
Perimeter means the distance all the way round one shape. Find the two side lengths of one rectangle, then add all four sides.
Each rectangle is 6 cm long and 3 cm wide, so go round: 6, 3, 6, 3.

solutions.reliable: Cutting the square in half gives two rectangles that are 6 cm long and $6 \div 2 = 3$ cm wide. The perimeter of one is $6 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 18$ cm. The transferable idea: when a shape is cut, each piece gets a new side along the cut, so you cannot just halve the perimeter.

whyOnTest: Cutting a shape changes perimeter in a way it does not change area, which is a common trap in Kangaroo geometry.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
